hints: Look closely at what has actually changed: one amino acid in the beta chain. Which level of structure is defined simply by the sequence of amino acids?

Remember that protein folding builds upwards. If the sequence changes, think about how hydrogen bonding between amino acids and interactions between R groups, plus the packing of the four chains together, could all be disturbed.
walkthrough:
**Start with primary structure**

Primary structure is just the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain, joined by peptide bonds.

Changing even one amino acid in the beta chain means the sequence is different, so primary structure is definitely affected.

**See how folding depends on sequence**

Secondary structure (alpha helices held by hydrogen bonds) and tertiary structure (precise 3D folding held by bonds between R groups such as hydrogen, ionic and hydrophobic interactions) both depend on which amino acids are present.

A different R group can form different bonds, so both secondary and tertiary structure of that beta chain could change.

**Check the whole haemoglobin molecule**

Quaternary structure is the association of the four polypeptides, two alpha and two beta chains, to make functional haemoglobin.

If a beta chain folds differently or is less stable, how the four chains fit and hold together will also be affected. So all four levels can be affected.

options.A: Primary is affected, but not only primary. Higher levels of folding depend on the sequence, so they can change too.
options.B: It is correct that primary and quaternary can change, but this misses secondary and tertiary folding of the beta chain, which also depend on the amino acid sequence.
options.C: Secondary, tertiary and quaternary can all change, but primary must also be included because the amino acid sequence itself is changed.
options.D: One amino acid change alters primary structure, and this can alter hydrogen bonding, R group interactions and chain packing, so secondary, tertiary and quaternary can all be affected.
